The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Assume countable choice. A dualizable framed handle link is an ordered
three-component link $(B,G,R)$ in
$S^3$ in which $R$ is designated as a dotted component representing a
$4$-dimensional $1$-handle, $B$ and $G$ are designated as $0$-framed $2$-handle
attaching circles (their framing pushoffs represent their preferred longitudes),
the ordered sublink $(B,R)$ is ambient isotopic as an
unframed link to $B$ together with a meridian of $B$, the ordered sublink
$(G,R)$ has the same property with $G$ in place of $B$, and
$\operatorname{lk}(B,G)=0$. Here $\operatorname{lk}(B,G)$ is half the sum of
the signs of the mixed crossings in any regular oriented diagram of $B\cup G$;
the linking-number lemma guarantees that this is an integer independent of the
chosen diagram. The associated handlebody
$X(B,G,R)$ has one
$0$-handle, the $1$-handle represented by $R$, and the two indicated
$2$-handles. Dotted-circle notation means that the unknotted component $R$
specifies a $1$-handle $D^1\times D^3$ attached along its two foot balls
$\partial D^1\times D^3$; its belt sphere is $\{0\}\times S^2$. A
$0$-framed $2$-handle is $D^2\times D^2$ attached along its attaching region

longitude.

The datum also includes the full framing gluing convention described below; quotient compatibility alone is insufficient. The band framing matches the classes of $(v_{i2},\ldots,v_{iq})$. Round the seams in the two-dimensional plane formed by the end disk's radial direction and the transverse band direction. This reflection concerns the copy used in the band sum; the retained handle $h_2$ keeps its original attaching embedding. In an oriented boundary, this is the usual condition that the orientations induced on the two removed end disks by the framed spheres and the band have opposite boundary-gluing signs. Both addition and subtraction are allowed by the choice of band-end coordinates and this sign convention.

The seam rotation in the indicated plane, together with the remaining band normal vectors, gives a full framing agreeing with the first old framing and the signed second-copy framing. A sufficiently thin normal thickening is then an attaching embedding; take the parallel copy outside the retained attaching region and the thickening small enough to be disjoint from it. For $k=1$, use the full normal framing transported when the chosen foot is pushed along the band and across the parallel interval core of $h_2$ to its other foot; this fixes the analogous sign convention without using a positive-dimensional seam. The displacement can be interpolated in the framed normal disk bundle without changing the prescribed parallel's framing.

Join $p$ to $q'$ by a smooth embedded arc $a$ in $\operatorname{int}D_R$ whose interior misses $G\cap D_R$, $q$, and $q'$. Such an arc is obtained by a polygonal path in the disk minus the finitely many forbidden points, removing loops in its finite subdivision and smoothing its corners in small disjoint disks. A thin strip about $a$ misses the remaining intersections and $B$. Choose the strip's normal product neighborhood so that the short branches of $G$ at $p$ and $B'$ at $q'$ are vertical, while its interior misses all three retained components. In its positive side, join short intervals of these vertical branches by an embedded band running just above $a$. Give the band its product framing and the full seam framing of [F2]. Band summing $G$ with $B'$ along it is one allowed slide over $B$; choose the sign of the parallel to make the oriented attachments agree. This sign does not change the underlying geometric construction.

One of the new band-sum arcs runs up from $p$, along one edge of the band, and down to $q'$. Together with a parallel of $a$ in $D_R$ it bounds an embedded disk in the positive product half-neighborhood. Its interior misses the slid circle and the retained components: the other edge of the band is chosen on the opposite transverse side of this disk, and the rest of $B'$ and $G$ misses the neighborhood. Push this arch across that disk and slightly into the negative side of $D_R$, rounding its ends. In strip coordinates this just replaces an arch above $z=0$ joining two points of $z=0$ by an arc below $z=0$; extend the motion to its thin tubular neighborhood. This is a link isotopy supported away from $B\cup R$. It removes precisely the intersections $p,q'$ and creates none, while all old intersections away from $p$ persist. Thus a slide followed by this isotopy changes $|G\cap D_R|$ from $N$ to $N+1-2=N-1$, regardless of their signs. No pairing of old opposite-sign intersections is needed. Transport the attaching framing by this isotopy.

Repeat steps 1.1–3.1 for the current attaching circle whenever an intersection remains. Each new parallel and strip can be chosen sufficiently thin for that finite stage, and the fixed $B,R,D_R$ are retained. The nonnegative integer intersection count drops by one at every stage, so after exactly the original number of intersections the current attaching circle is disjoint from $D_R$. The resulting finite sequence consists solely of the permitted framed slides and link isotopies and proves the full statement.

normal section and push $D$ slightly along it to a parallel disk $D'$ in the

class in $H_1(E_K)$ is zero. By [F2], it is the preferred longitude.

1.2 A tubular neighborhood of $D$ is $D^2\times D^2$ and meets the other
hemisphere $B_2$ in the attaching region $S^1\times D^2$. Consequently
$B_2\cup\nu(D)$ is obtained from a $4$-ball by attaching one $0$-framed
$2$-handle along $K$, hence is diffeomorphic to $X_0(K)$ by [F1]. This union
is a smooth codimension-zero submanifold of $S^4$.

2.1 Conversely, suppose $i:X_0(K)\hookrightarrow S^4$ is a smooth
codimension-zero embedding. In the $0$-handle of $X_0(K)$ take the cone on $K$
from an interior point $p$, and join that cone disk to the core disk
$D^2\times\{0}$ of the $2$-handle along their common boundary $K$. After
smoothing the join, this is a piecewise-smooth embedded $2$-sphere, smooth
away from the cone point $p$.

2.2 In oriented coordinates at $p$ and $i(p)$, the derivative of $i$ is
invertible by [F4], because its differential is injective and both dimensions
are four. By [F5], $i$ is a local diffeomorphism near $p$. If its local
orientation sign is negative, compose it with a fixed orientation-reversing
reflection of the standard $S^4$; this preserves the existence of the
embedding and makes the local sign positive. Thus its derivative $A$ lies in
$\mathrm{GL}^+(4,\mathbb R)$.

2.3 Identify the cone near $p$ with the radial cone on $K\subset S^3$. Along
each direction $u\in K$, the derivative at the cone point of the target
distance is $\lVert Au\rVert>0$. Compactness of $K$ makes this derivative
uniformly positive, so [F5] gives a smooth radial intersection parameter for
all sufficiently small target spheres. Taylor expansion in $C^1$ along $K$,
followed by radial normalization, makes the resulting link
$\Gamma_\epsilon$ $C^1$-close to $\phi_A(K)$, where
$\phi_A(u)=Au/\lVert Au\rVert$. The polar decomposition $A=QP$ joins $A$ to
the identity through $\mathrm{GL}^+(4,\mathbb R)$: join the positive-definite
$P$ to $I$ linearly and join $Q\in\mathrm{SO}(4)$ to $I$ by a path in the
connected group $\mathrm{SO}(4)$. Hence $\phi_A(K)$ is isotopic to $K$. The
chosen normal-disk tube of $K$, transported by $\phi_A$, is a tube of
$\phi_A(K)$. For sufficiently small $\epsilon$, the tubular projection
restricts to a local diffeomorphism from $\Gamma_\epsilon$ to $\phi_A(K)$.
It is homotopic to the identity because the curves are $C^1$-close, so it has
degree one; a local diffeomorphism of circles with degree one is a
diffeomorphism. Thus $\Gamma_\epsilon$ is the graph of a small normal section. Scaling that
section to zero gives a smooth knot isotopy to $\phi_A(K)$, so
$\Gamma_\epsilon$ is isotopic to $K$.

Let $C$ denote the Conway knot represented by the Conway diagram in Figure 1 of
Piccirillo's paper, and let $K_P$ denote the knot represented by the partner
diagram in Figure 2 of that paper. Choose an orientation on each diagram. The
symbols $C$ and $K_P$ refer to these specified diagram isotopy classes.

Assume countable choice. A dualizable framed handle link is an ordered
three-component link $(B,G,R)$ in
$S^3$ in which $R$ is designated as a dotted component representing a
$4$-dimensional $1$-handle, $B$ and $G$ are designated as $0$-framed $2$-handle
attaching circles (their framing pushoffs represent their preferred longitudes),
the ordered sublink $(B,R)$ is ambient isotopic as an
unframed link to $B$ together with a meridian of $B$, the ordered sublink
$(G,R)$ has the same property with $G$ in place of $B$, and
$\operatorname{lk}(B,G)=0$. Here $\operatorname{lk}(B,G)$ is half the sum of
the signs of the mixed crossings in any regular oriented diagram of $B\cup G$;
the linking-number lemma guarantees that this is an integer independent of the
chosen diagram. The associated handlebody
$X(B,G,R)$ has one
$0$-handle, the $1$-handle represented by $R$, and the two indicated
$2$-handles. Dotted-circle notation means that the unknotted component $R$
specifies a $1$-handle $D^1\times D^3$ attached along its two foot balls
$\partial D^1\times D^3$; its belt sphere is $\{0\}\times S^2$. A
$0$-framed $2$-handle is $D^2\times D^2$ attached along its attaching region
$S^1\times D^2$, with the boundary pushoff representing the preferred
longitude.

Assume countable choice. Let $(B,G,R)$ be a dualizable framed handle link and
let $X(B,G,R)$ be its associated handlebody. There are finite sequences of
handle slides and cancellations, first sliding $G$ over $B$ and cancelling
the $1$-handle $R$ with the $2$-handle $B$, and then using the reversed roles,
that leave single $0$-framed attaching knots $K_G$ and $K_B$, respectively.
There are diffeomorphisms
$$
X(B,G,R)\cong X_0(K_G)\cong X_0(K_B).
$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Let $C$ denote the Conway knot represented by the Conway diagram in Figure 1 of
Piccirillo's paper, and let $K_P$ denote the knot represented by the partner
diagram in Figure 2 of that paper. Choose an orientation on each diagram. The
symbols $C$ and $K_P$ refer to these specified diagram isotopy classes.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented link diagram with exactly one component, and let $c$ be its number of crossings. Perform the following construction in its projection sphere $S^2$.

1. Choose a point $q\in S^2$ outside the finite diagram. In pairwise disjoint small disks about the crossings, replace each crossing by the unique noncrossing smoothing compatible with the strand orientations. Let the resulting oriented circles be the Seifert circles and let $s$ be their number.
2. For each Seifert circle $C$, take the closure of the component of $S^2\setminus C$ that does not contain $q$. Under the stated choice axiom, each such region is an embedded compact disk. The finite family of disk regions is nested or disjoint. Orient each disk to induce the given orientation of its boundary circle, then place nested disks at distinct nearby heights ordered by inclusion; the resulting disk interiors are pairwise disjoint in $S^3$.
3. For every original crossing, attach one rectangular band along short boundary intervals on the two smoothing arcs. A half-twist means a single $180$-degree turn of the band across the crossing neighborhood. Choose its direction, endpoint orientations, and over/under order to match the original crossing.
4. Return the finite disk-and-band construction data together with $(s,c)$.

The returned data are a finite attached two-dimensional complex. This algorithm's definition alone does not assert that the resulting image is embedded, is a surface, is connected, or has the original knot as boundary; the separate correctness lemma establishes those properties.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every finite regular oriented diagram with exactly one component, the Seifert diagram procedure terminates after one finite smoothing scan and one finite band-record scan. It returns exactly one disk record for each Seifert circle and exactly one band record for each original crossing. Termination alone asserts no embeddedness, boundary equality, or genus minimality.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a single knot, and let the Seifert algorithm supply its finite disk-and-band construction data. These disks and bands can be realized in $S^3$ as a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface $F$ with exactly one boundary component, whose oriented boundary is the knot represented by $D$. The bands can be chosen mutually disjoint and disjoint from disk interiors except at their attaching intervals.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K:S^1\hookrightarrow S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere, and let $F\subset S^3$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, oriented so that its boundary orientation is the given orientation of $K$. Let $g$ be the nonnegative integer determined by $\chi(F)=1-2g$. Choose an ordered integral basis $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ of the first singular homology group $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, represented by integral one-cycles on $F$. Orient the normal line of $F$ by requiring $(n,u,v)$ to be positively oriented in $S^3$ whenever $(u,v)$ is a positive tangent basis of $F$. The positive push-off $a_i^+$ is the cycle carried to a sufficiently small positive normal level in a bicollar of $F$.

For disjoint oriented closed curves $J,L\subset S^3$, orient a meridian $\mu_L$ of $L$ so that a positive tangent to $L$ followed by a positive basis of its normal disk gives the ambient orientation. The linking number $\operatorname{lk}(J,L)$ is the integer determined by $[J]=\operatorname{lk}(J,L)[\mu_L]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus L;\mathbb Z)$, using the Alexander-duality identification that sends $[\mu_L]$ to $1$. Extend linking additively over integral one-cycles. The Seifert pairing is $\theta_F(x,y)=\operatorname{lk}(x^+,y)$, and its matrix in the chosen basis is $V=(V_{ij})_{i,j=1}^{2g}$, where $V_{ij}=\theta_F(a_i,a_j)=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The surface and basis are part of the data; this definition asserts no knot-only matrix invariant.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented embedded circle in the oriented standard three-sphere, let $F$ be a connected compact smooth oriented embedded surface with boundary $K$, and let $a_1,\ldots,a_{2g}$ be the ordered integral basis and positive normal push-off convention used to define the Seifert matrix $V$ above. Every class of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$ has a representative that is a finite integral sum of pairwise disjoint smooth oriented embedded circles in $F$. For such representatives $x$ and $y$, the sum of the pairwise linking numbers between the positive push-off of $x$ and $y$ depends only on $[x]$ and $[y]$, is independent of the sufficiently small positive push-off, and equals the bilinear extension of $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$. The linking number of two disjoint oriented circle components is symmetric. In particular, the Seifert pairing is a well-defined bilinear map $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\times H_1(F;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ and $J$ be disjoint oriented smooth
embedded circles in the oriented three-sphere, and let $\Sigma$ be a compact
oriented smooth surface embedded in the three-sphere with boundary $K$, whose
outward-normal-first boundary orientation is the specified orientation of $K$.
Here outward-normal-first means that an outward-pointing normal followed by a
positive boundary tangent gives the orientation of $\Sigma$. Assume
$J$ is transverse to $\Sigma$, and fix a regular oriented diagram $D$ of
$J\cup K$. Let $\eta$ be a positively oriented meridian of $K$ and let
$m\in\mathbb Z$ be the unique integer such that
$[J]=m[\eta]$ in $H_1(S^3\setminus K;\mathbb Z)$. Define the topological
linking number by $\operatorname{lk}(J,K):=m$. Let
$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)$ be the half-sum of the signs of the mixed crossings
of $D$. Orient the normal line of $\Sigma$ by the ambient orientation. A point
of $J\cap\Sigma$ has sign $+1$ if the oriented curve $J$ crosses from the
negative side of $\Sigma$ to its positive side, and sign $-1$ for the reverse
passage. Then
$$\operatorname{lk}_D(J,K)=\operatorname{lk}(J,K)=\sum_{p\in J\cap\Sigma}\operatorname{sign}_\Sigma(p).$$
The statement is conditional on a supplied spanning surface and regular
diagram; it asserts no surface- or diagram-existence theorem.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets (Finite, countably infinite, countable, uncountable) has a choice function.

Let $C$ denote the Conway knot represented by the Conway diagram in Figure 1 of
Piccirillo's paper, and let $K_P$ denote the knot represented by the partner
diagram in Figure 2 of that paper. Choose an orientation on each diagram. The
symbols $C$ and $K_P$ refer to these specified diagram isotopy classes.

**Input:** a nonempty finite regular oriented link diagram $D$ and a total order $c_1<\cdots<c_n$ on its crossing set. A diagram object is supplied as mathematical input; this procedure does not parse a serialized string.

**Output:** the normalized bigraded Khovanov cochain module $C^{i,j}(D)$ and its candidate differential $d:C^{i,j}(D)\to C^{i+1,j}(D)$, constructed by the following finite instructions.

1. Enumerate every state $v:C(D)\to\{0,1\}$ once. Form the crossingless resolution by using the A-smoothing at $v(c)=0$ and the B-smoothing at $v(c)=1$.
2. For each state, create one tensor factor of the integral Frobenius algebra for each resolution circle and place the resulting tensor product in cohomological degree $|v|-n_-$ and quantum degree $|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum\deg(a)$ for its circle labels $a$.
3. For each state and each crossing $c_j$ with $v(c_j)=0$, create the edge to $v+e_j$. Apply multiplication if that smoothing change merges two circles, comultiplication if it splits one circle, the identity on other tensor factors, and the sign $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v(c_i)}$. Sum the edge maps out of every state to obtain $d$.
4. Return the finite direct sum of the state modules with these degrees and maps. The square-zero property is the separate local lemma named by `justified_by`.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For an oriented knot $K$, let $V_K$ be its two-dimensional rational Lee homology with the diagram-independent induced decreasing quantum filtration $F^pV_K$. For a nonzero class $x\in V_K$, define its filtration level by
$$ \ell(x)=\max\{p\in\mathbb Z:x\in F^pV_K\}. $$
Set
$$ s_{\min}(K)=\min_{x\ne0}\ell(x),\qquad s_{\max}(K)=\max_{x\ne0}\ell(x), \qquad s(K)=s_{\max}(K)-1=s_{\min}(K)+1. $$
The equality of the two formulas is part of the definition’s well-definedness, supplied by the rank-two Lee filtration theorem.

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented link diagram in the standard oriented $3$-sphere. Use the oriented Khovanov resolution cube, crossing order, signs, and shifts fixed in the integral Khovanov construction. Over $\mathbb Q$, replace its circle algebra by $A_L=\mathbb Q[X]/(X^2-1)$, with $\deg_q(1)=1$ and $\deg_q(X)=-1$, and structure maps
$$
\eta_L(1)=1,\quad \epsilon_L(1)=0,\quad \epsilon_L(X)=1,
$$
$$
m_L(1\otimes1)=1,\quad m_L(1\otimes X)=m_L(X\otimes1)=X,\quad m_L(X\otimes X)=1,
$$
$$
\Delta_L(1)=1\otimes X+X\otimes1,\quad \Delta_L(X)=1\otimes1+X\otimes X.
$$
For a resolution state $v$ with $k(v)$ circles, assign $A_L^{\otimes k(v)}$ and cohomological degree $i(v)=|v|-n_-$. On a tensor basis element whose circle labels are $a_1,\ldots,a_{k(v)}\in\{1,X\}$, set
$$
q(v;a_1,\ldots,a_{k(v)})=|v|+n_+-2n_-+\sum_{j=1}^{k(v)}\deg_q(a_j).
$$
The differential is the signed sum of the edge maps $m_L$ and $\Delta_L$. The resulting finite cochain complex is the **Lee-deformed Khovanov complex** $C_L(D;\mathbb Q)$. Its decreasing quantum filtration $F^pC_L(D;\mathbb Q)$ is spanned by basis elements of quantum degree at least $p$. Its homology with the induced filtration is the Lee homology of the diagram. The diagram-level definition does not by itself assert invariance under changing $D$.

The two equal composites in the diagram below are the Frobenius compatibility maps used on merge-split faces. The drawing names maps only; the proof checks the equality on the basis $\{1,X\}^{\otimes2}$.

```tikzcd
A_L\otimes A_L \arrow[r,"m_L"] \arrow[d,"\Delta_L\otimes\mathrm{id}"'] & A_L \arrow[d,"\Delta_L"] \\
A_L\otimes A_L\otimes A_L \arrow[r,"\mathrm{id}\otimes m_L"'] & A_L\otimes A_L
```

In the original $5323\times1843$ image its eleven crossing centers are approximately $(1540,216),(310,538),(1867,633),(1335,806),(877,840),(175,919),(884,1180),(375,871),(410,1527),(1890,1393),(1443,1230)$, in this order. Starting at the underpass of crossing $2$ toward crossing $8$, its complete cyclic visit word is $U2,O8,U7,U11,O10,O9,U6,O2,U5,O7,U9,O6,U8,O5,O4,U3,O1,U4,O11,U10,O3,U1$. Number outgoing arcs successively $0,\ldots,21$. Following these literal source strands with convention [F5] gives $[(20,15,21,16),(21,6,0,7),(14,19,15,20),(16,13,17,14),(7,12,8,13),(5,11,6,10),(1,9,2,8),(11,1,12,0),(9,5,10,4),(18,4,19,3),(2,18,3,17)]$. All eleven source underpass gaps are used, while the three extra breaks at the red mutation circle are simply joined. Use these eleven crossings in their listed order. The local PD quadruple is counterclockwise from the incoming under-arc. Its zero smoothing joins positions $(0,1),(2,3)$ and its one smoothing joins $(0,3),(1,2)$. With the oriented visit word there are six positive and five negative crossings, so the normalized cohomological and quantum shifts are $|v|-5$ and $|v|-4$. Reversing the single component changes neither crossing signs nor these shifts. This input is the selected Conway diagram, not a table entry or a polynomial-based identification.

Form the finite rational cube [F2] on these two exact inputs. A reproducible rank calculation enumerates the smoothing circles as equivalence classes of arc labels under the two local pairings in step 1.1, orders the circles by their least arc, and labels a tensor by the bit string whose $1$ bits carry $X$. On an edge changing crossing $j$, use the sign $(-1)^{\sum_{i<j}v_i}$ and the merge or split map. For Khovanov cohomology set $m(X,X)=0$ and omit the $1\otimes1$ term of $\Delta(X)$; for Lee use all terms in [F6]. In each quantum degree, exact rational Gaussian elimination gives $\dim Kh^{h,q}=\dim C^{h,q}-\operatorname{rank}d^{h,q}-\operatorname{rank}d^{h-1,q}$. The complete resulting rational rank polynomials, grouped by $h$, are the two tables below. They were computed independently on these PDs by the characteristic-one command `-ku1` in KnotJob, where `1` denotes rational coefficients, not a finite field. Its arithmetic stores reduced integer numerator/denominator pairs; zero tests and inversions are exact. Tensoring a crossing at a time and cancelling invertible differentials is an efficient realization of the same finite Gaussian calculation: for a pivot $u:C_a\to C_b$, deleting $a,b$ and replacing a remaining coefficient by $d_{cd}-d_{cb}u^{-1}d_{ad}$ splits off the contractible two-term summand. The elementary basis changes proving this identity are invertible over $\mathbb Q$, so the operation preserves the computed cohomology. The Conway rank polynomial was also independently recomputed with the integral cube implementation `cppkh`; its free ranks give exactly the same rational table. Thus neither table is a quoted invariant value from the literature.

For the only additional Conway Lee calculation needed, retain homological degrees $-2,-1,0,1,2$ of its direct cube, with the operations [F6]. This truncation preserves degrees $-1,0,1$ and their induced first spectral-sequence differential: their kernels and images involve exactly these adjacent chain degrees. It has $18,246$ enhanced-state basis elements and $119,684$ initial nonzero differential entries. Direct multiplication checks $d^2=0$, and every entry raises quantum degree by $0$ or $4$. Cancel degree-zero invertible arrows by the Schur rule of step 2.1, using the increasing initial basis-index order for the queue, and append every newly created degree-zero arrow to its end. Each such cancellation is filtered, since the paired basis vectors have equal quantum degree. There are $8,038$ cancellations. In homological degrees $-1,0,1$ the remaining generators are precisely $q^{-3}+q^{-1}+2q$, $2q^{-1}+3q+q^3$, and $q+2q^3+q^5$, as independently verified by the rational table. The transferred degree-four differential from the one-dimensional group $Kh^{-1,-1}(C)$ to the one-dimensional group $Kh^{0,3}(C)$ is the matrix $(2/3)$. This exact entry results from the above rational Schur updates; the standard-library calculation in the accompanying family source `conway-lee-computation.py` specifies every state, sign, entry and cancellation and asserts the matrix identity. In particular this is a nonzero differential into quantum degree $3$, so that class does not survive.

In the partner table, $Kh^{0,*}=\mathbb Q_{-1}\oplus\mathbb Q_1^2\oplus\mathbb Q_3$, $Kh^{-1,*}=\mathbb Q_1^2$, and $Kh^{1,*}=\mathbb Q_1^2\oplus\mathbb Q_3^3\oplus\mathbb Q_5$. The degree-three class cannot support or receive any Lee differential: the possible outgoing bidegrees are $(1,3+4k)$ and incoming bidegrees $(-1,3-4k)$ for integers $k\ge1$, and all of these groups are zero by the table. The multiple-of-four restriction follows from [F6] and the quantum congruence decomposition; a finite filtration makes these all possible pages. Thus the degree-three class survives. The two limiting levels lie in $\{-1,1,3\}$, differ by two and include $3$, so they are exactly $(1,3)$. Therefore [F4] gives $s(K_P)=2$. Notice that the incoming test is $3-4k$, not $-3-4k$; the latter expression occurs in the 2018 arXiv preprint, while the published 2020 proof gives the correct incoming bidegree. The independent characteristic-zero `-s0` calculation also returns $2$ on this exact input.

The complete Conway $h=0$ row has quantum degrees only $-1,1,3$. By step 3.1 the last is removed on the first possible nonzero Lee differential. Every later page is a subquotient of the corresponding previous bidegree, so no new degree can appear. The two nonzero limiting quantum levels are therefore $-1,1$: by [F3] they occur in two different congruence classes modulo four and differ by two, and Lee homology has dimension two. Hence [F4] gives $s(C)=0$. As an independent arithmetic check, the unmodified rational `s` calculation in knotkit and the characteristic-zero `-s0` calculation in KnotJob both return $0$ on the same diagram; these outputs are not needed in place of the explicit nonzero differential.

Steps 4.1 and 3.2 give the asserted rational Lee filtration levels $(-1,1)$ and $(1,3)$ on the two diagrams specified in [F1]. The tables in step 2.1 provide the full rational Khovanov ranks used in this calculation, while step 3.1 supplies the additional actual Lee differential required for Conway. The bounded spectral sequence in [F3] has no further page capable of changing either conclusion. Together these prove every part of the Statement.
